newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Primakov emerges from NATO in relaxed mood.
newsitem.headline: Primakov emerges from NATO in relaxed mood.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Wednesday welcomed NATO's offer of talks on improving ties in future but made clear Moscow still bitterly opposed the alliance's expansion plans.

Primakov held an hour of talks with NATO foreign ministers during which officials said it was clear he had tried hard to balance Russia's unhappiness over the enlargement programme with its desire to formalise a relationship with the alliance.
The Russian minister, best known for his taciturn and clipped style, was in unusually relaxed mood afterwards and even found time for a few deadpan asides.

Primakov said Moscow had agreed to an offer from NATO to discuss issues of concern but reiterated Russia's opposition to expansion of the alliance on the grounds that it would lead to new divisions in Europe.

"We were made an offer to hold consultations with NATO in order to settle any issues that might be of concern to us. We agreed to this offer. I think this will open the door to fruitful talks," he told a news conference.

"Of course, we do not like the expansion of NATO's military infrastructure towards our territory. We are against this and are looking for solutions, one of which is a dialogue which I hope will now begin."
NATO has made it quite clear that nothing can prevent its plans to offer membership to former central and east European states which were once key Kremlin allies.

Alliance officials are therefore urging Moscow to come to its senses and make the most of the situation by agreeing to map out the course of future relations, first of all by opening discussions on what both sides might want.

"I think this will allow us to move forwards and Russia, despite its dislike of enlargement, will continue to regard NATO as an important organisation with real power. We of course will be pragmatic when dealing with it," said Primakov.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana wants to conclude an agreement on future ties with Russia before an alliance summit next July formally invites a handful of countries to start talks on membership.

"Today a document, if there is to be one, needs specific provisions which remove our concerns. We will strive towards that," said Primakov, adding that agreeing a general declaration of principles would be "a train to nowhere".
And in another sign that Moscow wants a good relationship with NATO, Primakov deftly dodged a question on how Russia viewed the alliance's various internal disputes and squabbles.
"I do not want our dialogue with NATO to start with us analysing these arguments or using them to further our own interests," he said with a smile.
Asked how he found dealing with Solana, who beamed broadly throughout the joint news conference, Primakov replied:

"You know, I have good relations with the secretary-general and I try to ensure things stay that way. He is a very nice man. But I would not use all those terms to describe the organisation which he heads."
